title: Wren and the Contact
premise: Quentin Eriksen's latest contract—guarding a whistleblower named Wren Vasquez in a Rotterdam safe house—collapses when a real-estate listing exposes the house's interior, including a hidden room where Wren stashed evidence of a tri-national arms laundering scheme. Hunted by an assassin called Marrow and disavowed by the agency that hired him, Quentin must smuggle Wren and the files across three borders while deciding whether to sell the truth to the highest bidder or burn his own carefully constructed life to deliver it for free. The climax comes at a decommissioned lighthouse on the Danish coast, where Quentin trades himself to Marrow to buy Wren time to broadcast the files; he survives, barely, but loses the clean identity he'd spent a decade building. In the end, justice arrives outside any courtroom, and Quentin—nameless now, finally honest—chooses to stay in Wren's orbit rather than vanish again.
about_author: Rosalind Underhill is a former maritime insurance investigator who spent eleven years auditing cargo routes through Northern European ports before turning to fiction. She writes thrillers about people whose jobs require them to be unmemorable, and she still keeps a go-bag out of habit.

chapters.title: The Polished Lie
chapters.summary: Quentin Eriksen's POV. We meet him mid-routine: rotating safe houses, a go-bag by the door, a fabricated biography rehearsed until it feels true. His client, Wren Vasquez, is prickly, sleepless, and convinced someone is watching. The emotional beat is quiet unease—the sense that Quentin's competence is a mask wearing thin.

chapters.title: Listing 4B
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Scrolling property sites at 3 a.m., Wren finds their safe house listed for sale—with interior photos showing the hidden crawl space where they've cached encrypted drives. Panic sets in; they wake Quentin. The beat is dread: the walls of their sanctuary have been photographed, measured, and offered to strangers.

chapters.title: Open House
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Posing as a buyer, Quentin attends the listing's open house and recognizes the 'realtor' as a spotter for Marrow, a methodical assassin with a reputation for finishing contracts after everyone else quits. He extracts Wren hours before the surveillance team returns. Beat: adrenaline sharpening into cold clarity.

chapters.title: The Agency That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin calls his handler for extraction and gets a dead line, then a second call offering triple pay to hand over 'the asset.' He realizes the contracting firm has sold them both. Beat: betrayal—the professional scaffolding of his life revealed as rot.

chapters.title: What Wren Stole
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren decrypts enough of the cache to explain it: shipping manifests proving three governments laundered arms through humanitarian corridors. They argue over what to do with it—sell it, leak it, use it as a shield. Beat: friction between survival instinct and conscience.

chapters.title: Marrow
chapters.summary: Marrow's POV, first time. A patient, almost tender killer reviews the listing photos like family albums, noting which rooms Quentin guarded well and which he neglected. Marrow respects craft. Beat: chilling intimacy—we see the hunt from inside the hunter.

chapters.title: Antwerp Detour
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. A planned ferry escape collapses when their cover documents flag at the terminal; Quentin burns his primary legend and reroutes them overland through Antwerp's docklands, calling in a favor from a retired colleague who charges a dangerous price: a name. Beat: the cost of trust begins accruing.

chapters.title: The Price of a Name
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren learns what Quentin gave up—the name of another protected client—to buy their passage, and confronts him about spending other people's safety. Their first real argument doubles as the first real honesty between them. Beat: guilt and the ethics of triage.

chapters.title: Three Governments, One Inbox
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin tests the waters, anonymously offering fragments of the files to journalists and officials in all three countries; two responses are entrapment attempts, one is genuine but terrified. He learns the truth has no safe buyer. Beat: disillusionment with institutions.

chapters.title: Safe House Rules
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Holed up in a canal barge, Wren and Quentin establish improvised rules—shifts, lies they won't tell each other, signals. Domesticity blooms in the cracks of danger. Beat: tentative belonging, two people building a home that can't last.

chapters.title: The Retired Colleague
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. The colleague who sold his name turns up dead, staged as a burglary, and Quentin understands Marrow is erasing the trail backward toward them. Grief he didn't expect surfaces for a man he only half-trusted. Beat: mourning complicity.

chapters.title: Border Crossing
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A night crossing into Germany goes wrong when a checkpoint guard recognizes Wren's face from a circulated alert; Quentin talks them through with a forged manifest and sheer nerve, but Wren sees how easily he lies—and wonders if they're just another client. Beat: intimacy shadowed by doubt.

chapters.title: What Quentin Buried
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Flashback chapter: the operation years ago where Quentin followed orders, looked away, and a village paid the price—the origin of his polished lie and his packed bag. He tells Wren none of this yet. Beat: the reader learns the debt driving him.

chapters.title: Marrow's Offer
chapters.summary: Marrow's POV. Marrow corners Quentin alone in a Hamburg parking structure—not to kill him, but to hire him: walk away, and the firm will let him live with his savings intact. Marrow genuinely likes his work. Beat: temptation framed as respect.

chapters.title: Refusal
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin declines, and Marrow gives him seventy-two hours before the contract reactivates. Quentin returns to the barge and finally tells Wren the truth about the village, the lie, the bag always packed. Beat: confession as turning point—he stops running from himself.

chapters.title: The Broadcast Problem
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Leaking the files requires a hardline uplink and forty uninterrupted minutes—impossible while hunted. Wren proposes the decommissioned Skagen lighthouse, offline-grid, one road in. Quentin maps the kill box and hates every angle of it. Beat: desperate hope hardening into a plan.

chapters.title: Seventy-Two Hours
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Preparations montage: buying time with false trails, wiring decoy drives, teaching Wren to finish the upload without him. Each task is a goodbye neither names. Beat: tenderness under fatalism.

chapters.title: Skagen
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Arrival at the lighthouse through fog; the sea hammering below. Wren begins the upload as headlights appear on the single road. Beat: dread and resolve—the point of no return.

chapters.title: The Lighthouse
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Climax. Quentin meets Marrow on the gallery deck and offers the trade: himself for the forty minutes. A brutal close-quarters fight among the lamp machinery; Quentin takes wounds that will mark him forever but holds the door. Beat: sacrifice as redemption in motion.

chapters.title: Forty Minutes
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Interleaved with the fight below, Wren watches the progress bar crawl—99% as gunshots echo up the stairwell. The files publish worldwide. Marrow withdraws, contract voided by exposure, honoring some private code. Beat: triumph inseparable from terror.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Hospitals, inquiries, three governments scrambling; Quentin's legends are all burned, his accounts frozen, his old employer indicted. He is legally nobody—which, for the first time, feels like freedom. Beat: raw convalescence and strange lightness.

chapters.title: Unpacked
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, closing. Months later, in a rented flat above a Copenhagen bakery, Wren finds Quentin's go-bag unpacked into drawers—his choice, unstated. Two people who guarded themselves against belonging finally belong somewhere small and undefended. Beat: quiet, earned peace.
